# Water and Hydrogen

## Core ideas and reasoning

Water is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen with formula H₂O. Its bent molecule and polar bonds help explain its solvent behaviour and hydrogen bonding between molecules. Tests include anhydrous copper(II) sulfate changing from white to blue and blue cobalt chloride paper turning pink. These show water is present but do not prove a sample is pure. Pure water has characteristic boiling and freezing temperatures at specified pressure. Hydrogen can be prepared by reacting a suitable metal such as zinc with dilute acid in supervised laboratory conditions. Discard the initial gas-air mixture before testing small samples because hydrogen mixed with air is flammable. Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop in a small test. Collecting over water is suitable because it is only slightly soluble. Hydrogen can reduce some metal oxides to metal on heating, forming water; relate this to relative reactivity rather than assuming every oxide is reduced. Balance equations by conserving atoms, not by changing chemical formulas.

## Worked practice

### Example 1

State a chemical test for water.

Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate changes from white to blue when water is added. This demonstrates presence, not purity.

### Example 2

Write the equation for zinc reacting with dilute hydrochloric acid.

Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl₂(aq) + H₂(g). One mole of zinc produces one mole of hydrogen.

### Example 3

Why can hydrogen be collected over water?

It is only slightly soluble in water and does not react significantly with it under the collection conditions.

## Check your reasoning

Explain why the method applies before calculating or naming a result. Compare with a contrasting case. For calculations carry units, keep intermediate precision, then check by substitution, conservation or a second route. Describe observations separately from their explanation.
